bet.text: Drive physically faster: the team says it realized early that this was the easiest way to shorten cycles at a higher level, and built a 12-motor swerve drive.

demand.text: Cubes first: the team acquired them much faster than cones and preferred them, though it called itself fast at both.
At the championship the lead mentor called cones its weak spot. With most cubes covered, and the supply of cubes running out, its alliance sought third and fourth robots that could do cones.
An observer credits the winning alliance with shuffling cubes across the field into hybrid nodes.

auto.text: Before an off-season rework it had been doing "two mids and a high" in auto.
One table gives it 2.0 auto pieces and 14.8 auto points per championship qualification match.

cycle.text: A cube passes through the wide elevator into the claw, or the claw takes a cone. The operator presses a button for one of 27 scoring locations; the robot generates a path and an elevator command. A cone is dropped straight down onto the node. Once the piece has left, the elevator lowers by itself.

gave_up.text: Battery: the team called itself incredibly battery limited, set current limits only to finish a match without brownouts, and used the whole battery.
The lead mentor says it made a lot of compromises for that drivetrain, and that the collisions drew many red cards, especially at its first event.
It stayed at maximum weight, to drive straight without going around congestion.

changed.text: Falcon v3 motors drew far more current and were instantly swapped back to v2.1.
The cube intake was a late addition.
On 28 March, when a poster called it a mid-season drivetrain change, the team said everything but the elevator got some rework from it.
After two regionals the arm pivot got a second motor for "the crawl".
Off-season: a 1323-style arm and wrist replaced the four-bar.

outcome.text: 60-10-1 in official play; won the Hopper division; pick 1 of the Hopper alliance on Einstein; won the championship; ranked 31 by championship OPR (68.05, Hopper).

functions.name: 12-motor swerve

solves.text: Shorten cycles by driving faster, in a straight line across the field without going around congestion

functions.type: swerve with two drive motors per module

facts.text: SDS MK4i modules with a custom top plate; the second drive motor meshes with the same main drive gear
Motors on the robot, all Falcons, 12 of them on the drive
A 25-tooth pinion meshes both motors with a 50-tooth gear without a custom SDS bottom plate; L2 or L3 gears with it would be geared too high
The pinion is a standard hex-bore gear on a Falcon spline adapter
Hypothetical top speed, about (automatic captions)
The first module was a clip-on unit, made before the team knew whether it was any good or left enough motors
FOC on the motors, which the team says allows lower and lighter gear ratios
Weight without bumpers
Frame 26x26, against 30x30 in 2022, so it could not afford the 1 in module inset of 2022; rails are 2x1

cost.text: Tuned to run about 2:45 to 3:00 before browning out on v2.1 Falcons
With v3 Falcons the team saw around 150% more current and about 50 s before browning out; it does not know why

functions.name: Continuous belt elevator

solves.text: Lift with a compact gearbox and little maintenance

functions.type: slanted continuous elevator with belts inside the tubes

facts.text: Reduction to a 36-tooth pulley and 18 mm wide HTD5 belt
Two motors, packaged in line with the bottom 2x2 to maximize travel and overlap
Belts run between the stages inside the tubes, after 971 in 2011, 2910 in 2018 and 1323 in 2019; redirects are kept few
WCP inline bearing blocks with 0.75 in bearings on all surfaces, after many small bearings cracked or wore into tubes
Idlers have no teeth, so the belt wraps a radius below its maker's minimum with less friction
A machined block and cam tension the belt; four 10-32 screws clamp it to the 2x1
Four constant-force springs pull the middle stages down because of the pass-over; the slant also reduces the help from gravity
Aim: bearing centers always this far apart, more than
Stage stops cut from aluminum bent; stainless steel ones held

cost.text: A huge upfront investment that takes precision and careful assembly
Three to four sets of constant-force springs over the season; the team's least favorite part of the elevator
The team says it is not low-hanging fruit: most teams would gain more from commercial parts and a better scoring subsystem

functions.name: Virtual non-parallel four-bar arm

solves.text: Take cones that stand up or lie tipped towards the robot, and reach feeder and scoring positions, with one arm motion

functions.type: chain virtual four-bar with a roller claw

facts.text: Sprockets of different size at each end turn the claw through the arm's motion
Turnbuckles on each side tune the angles
Cones are dropped straight down onto the node, for more precise scoring
The stow angle keeps the center of gravity low when crossing the field
The pivot uses 20 DP gears to save weight
Two motors on the pivot and one on the claw; the second pivot motor came after the first two regionals, so the arm could lift the robot for "the crawl"

solves.text: Make cube cycles faster than any others and hand the cube to the claw

facts.text: The wide elevator leaves room for the cube to pass through
Rollers, tapes and plain Lexan sections guide the cube into the claw
One motor for the rollers and one for the pivot

functions.name: Button board and auto drive

solves.text: Make scoring as fast and easy as possible for the drivers

functions.type: operator-selected auto drive with on-the-fly trajectories

facts.text: Buttons, one per scoring location
A press gives a pose, a trajectory from the current velocity and heading, and the elevator command for that height
Three Limelights give almost 180 degrees of view; the camera with the largest target area is used
Position comes from a pinhole model of the distance to each tag, fused with odometry in WPILib's SwerveDrivePoseEstimator
The pinhole model gave far better results than Limelight's 3D tag tracking
A poster saw green lights while it placed cones and assumed retroreflective targets were used at some point; another says it used AprilTags
Off-season, a tower was added for more reliable tracking of the retroreflective tape and a back-facing Limelight, previously difficult on the low side of the slanted elevator
Sensors on the arm and in the intake detect cones and cubes; the elevator lowers by itself when the piece is gone, or once one is held at the feeder
It did not use vision to detect cones and cubes

cost.text: The team calls it one of its lowest-return optimizations: a straight-line PID drive took about 10% of the effort in the off-season and did as well, at times better

decisions.because: driving faster was the easiest way to shorten cycles, and a lack of endgame left motors to play with
decisions.cost: the team was incredibly battery limited

decisions.because: the advantage was driving straight across without going around congestion
decisions.instead_of: a lighter, faster robot, such as 90 lb at 25 fps
decisions.cost: a lighter robot would be much more forgiving on the battery

decisions.because: it is compact, and rigid belts in the tubes are easy to rig
decisions.instead_of: chain, cable or cord in the tubes
decisions.cost: a large upfront effort in precision and assembly

decisions.choice: Generate a trajectory to the node
decisions.because: it handled edge cases better, such as a driver fully at the wrong node when auto drive starts
decisions.instead_of: driving directly to the target, biased PID gains, or a point a few feet in front

decisions.because: most cubes were covered and the alliance was running out of cubes
